nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name:  permit
Scientific Name: Trachinotus falcatus

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum:  Chordata
	Class:  Osteichthyes
	Order:  Perciformes
	Family:  Carangidae

Other Common Names:  round pompano (312 581 834).

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  No directed fishery exist, and reported to be much less important then pompano (788).  About 90% of the total Florida catch of 118 tons in 1975 came from the west coast (791).  Caught in beach seines, purse seines, and gillnets (791).  Mostly sold fresh iced with edibility for small fish said to be excellent (791).  Snelson (997) reports that in the northern Indian River Lagoon permit are found seasonally in the commercial fishery.

Recreational:  Considered to be an important game fish, and classed as such in Florida (788).  Sportfish catches represent from 25 to 250 percent of the total commercial catch in Florida (791).  Caught throughout the year, although greatest numbers are taken in the spring and summer (214).  Caught on spinning rods and fly rods with live or artificial bait (791).  Larger fish are said to be very good when properly prepared (791).

nodes.title: Indicator
nodes.body: Ecological Role:  Important reef and surf zone predator (1272).

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  From Massachusetts to southern Brazil (327 788 791 846).  Young found in the Gulf Stream occasionally as far north as Cape Cod (214).  Common from North Carolina southward (214).  Reported to be uncommon or absent in estuaries of the northern Gulf of Mexico (255 581).  Also Bermuda (791), the Bahamas (788), and common throughout the West Indies (363 788 791).

Within Study Area:  Found throughout Florida waters.

Mobility and Migration:

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body: Larvae are pelagic (206 210).  Adults are also pelagic and epibenthic (791).  They tend to be solitary, but also known to school, perhaps for spawning (791).

nodes.title: Movements/Migration
nodes.body: In Tampa Bay, there is an apparent movement into and out of the Bay, with the greatest abundance in the spring and summer (214).

nodes.title: BENTHIC HABITAT
nodes.body:
Habitat Type:  Pelagic larvae are marine and are usually found offshore (206 210).  Young are marine and are frequently found in the surf (327).  Adults occur from shallow water to about 36 m depth (791).

Substrate:  Sandy flats, near reefs, and occasionally over mud bottoms (363 791 932).  Juveniles have been found in seagrass beds and associated with detritus (Breeder 1969).

nodes.title: Eggs/Larvae
nodes.body: Juvenile/adults:  Young from 18 to 44 mm are found on the beaches when water temperatures warm to about 27  C, and remain until temperatures cool to around 19.5  C (363).  Juveniles have been taken in temperatures from 16.4 to 34.0 C (603 886).  Adults have been shown to survive temperatures as low as 9.7 C for short periods, but temperatures below 15 C are generally unfavorable (214).  In Tampa Bay, specimens have been collected at temperatures from 15.8 to 33.7 C (214 664).  Wang and Raney (789) collected them at temperatures from 31.6 to 33.0 C in Charlotte Harbor.  Gunter and Hall collected them at temperatures from 21.6 to 30.7 C in the St. Lucie Estuary (264).  In the Indian River Lagoon (IRL), permit have been reported in cold kills with temperatures that went down to 6 C (997 236).  Christensen (887) reported that the juvenile coloration is much better suited for life on the grass flats then sandy beaches.

nodes.title: Eggs/Larvae
nodes.body: Juvenile/adults:  Juveniles collected at salinities ranging from 0.% (214) to 43.9 % (264 603 887).  Young were taken in Charlotte Harbor at salinities of 32.0 to 34.8 % (789).  Springer and Woodburn (664) collected specimens at 33.3 to 35.1 % in Tampa Bay.  Reported to occur in Tampa Bay from 23.0 to 35.6 %, but 85% were taken above 31 % (214 363).  Adults were collected in Charlotte Harbor at a salinity of 34.2 % (789).   Christensen (887) collected juveniles from 4.5ppt. to 37.2 ppt. in the Indian River Lagoon near Jupiter, Florida.

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode:  Broadcast spawning with external fertilization.
Mating & spawning:  Spawning apparently occurs offshore (206 210 214), possibly in or near the Gulf Stream (210) and Florida Current (1015).  A spring spawning period has been suggested in the Tampa Bay area (214 664).  May spawn from December through September with peak spawning from April to June (206 214) and a smaller peak in the summer or early fall (214).  Small specimens taken off North Carolina in January may indicate some winter spawning (206).

Fecundity:  No information available.

nodes.title: Eggs/Larvae
nodes.body: Juveniles/Adults:  Johnson (363) considered fish larger than 7.0 mm as juveniles.  Rapid growth rates have been reported with monthly growth of 15 to 20mm during the first year (214).  In Tampa Bay, Springer and Woodburn (664) reported specimens ranging from 8.2 to 19.8 mm in June to between 63.6 to 109.6 mm in November (664).  Length-weight relationships for juveniles and adults were given by Finucane (214).  Maximum size reported as 114 cm and 23 kg (788).  Solomon and Naughton found juveniles from August to January.

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: Considered a bottom feeder (664).  Juveniles eat a variety of benthic invertebrates (791).  Adult diet includes worms, crustaceans (crabs and shrimp), mollusks, and small fish (214 312 791).
